slides.content: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И КОМПЈУТЕРСКО ИНЖЕНЕРСТВО ..continued

slides.title: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И
slides.content: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И КОМПЈУТЕРСКО ИНЖЕНЕРСТВО 4.Gantt Charts In the late 19th century, Gantt charts were the gold standard, and are often the go-to business process model for companies preparing for projects with distinct timelines, or that have time- sensitive processes that need to be captured and tracked. Gantt charts make it easy for people involved in different parts of a process to see when they are meant to start work, and by when each task should be complete, and to check whether all the subprocesses are on schedule. Gantt charts are simplistic diagrams that provide a visualization of the overall time taken to complete a task or process. More specifically, Gantt charts can show the start and end times/dates of a process, the required tasks, and how long each took to complete. Rather than showing the steps sequentially, Gantt charts are able to show the entire process using ‘time taken’ as one of the main axes. It does a better job of showing the overall time taken to complete a project than other options.

slides.title: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И
slides.content: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И КОМПЈУТЕРСКО ИНЖЕНЕРСТВО ..continued

slides.title: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И
slides.content: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И КОМПЈУТЕРСКО ИНЖЕНЕРСТВО 5. Workflow Technique Workflow is a flow of tasks between computer applications or people in an organization. Two or more members of a workgroup to reach a common goal can define a workflow as well as any task performed in series or in parallel. The work flow is more than a technique to model a process. It is a method to analyze and improve a process, including its modeling. The workflow development process uses workflow models to capture the relevant information of the processes. This process comprises four stages: Information Gathering, Business Process Modelling, Workflow Modelling, Implementation and Verification & Execution.

slides.title: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И
slides.content: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И КОМПЈУТЕРСКО ИНЖЕНЕРСТВО 6.Data Flow Diagrams Data flow diagrams (DFDs) show how data enters a system from external sources, how data moves internally within the system, and how the data is stored. DFD symbols vary slightly, but are mostly based on the same principles:  Squares. These show external entities, which are either the source of data, or the destination  Rounded rectangles. These represent processes that receive data as input, interact with it, and then produce an output  Arrows. These show the flow of data, either as electronic data or physical items  Open-ended rectangles. This represents data stores, and include electronic stores like databases or XML files, as well as physical stores, such as or filing cabinets or stacks of paper

slides.title: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И
slides.content: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И КОМПЈУТЕРСКО ИНЖЕНЕРСТВО 7.Role Activity Diagrams Role activity diagrams (RADs) are used to map out the intangible roles or ideas of behaviour that are desired within the company. These can often be functions within the business, systems in IT, or customer and supplier roles. RADs are easy to read and understand, and often provide a different perspective on a process, which helps support communication. A RAD shows the roles that play a part in the process, and their component actions and interactions, together with external events and the logic that determines which actions are carried out when. So, it shows the activity of roles in the process and how they collaborate.

slides.content: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И КОМПЈУТЕРСКО ИНЖЕНЕРСТВО ..continued

slides.content: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И КОМПЈУТЕРСКО ИНЖЕНЕРСТВО 8.Role Interaction Diagrams Interaction diagrams are business process models that graphically illustrate the interaction of various processes with each other within a system. Interaction diagrams come in two forms: sequence diagrams and collaboration diagrams. There are two types of interaction diagrams typically used to capture the various aspects of interaction in a system: Sequence diagrams  Collaboration diagram 

slides.title: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И
slides.content: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И КОМПЈУТЕРСКО ИНЖЕНЕРСТВО ..continued Sequence diagrams A sequence diagram shows the interaction between objects in the sequence in which they take place. Sequence diagrams describe how the objects function within a system, and in what order, and are often used to document and understand what is required for new and existing systems

slides.title: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И
slides.content: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И КОМПЈУТЕРСКО ИНЖЕНЕРСТВО ..continued Collaboration diagram Collaboration diagrams are used to define and clarify the roles of the objects that carry out a certain flow of events in a visual format, and serve as the main source of information when determining class responsibilities and interfaces

There are 15 forms of IDEF and each addresses a different type of flow for functions, information, data, simulation model design, process description capture, and so on.

Object oriented methods The object oriented method of business process modelling is more than just modelling with objects: it encompasses message-passing, encapsulation (where internal detail is hidden), inheritance from class to subclass, and polymorphism (where the same procedure can operate on different data types).

slides.title: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И
slides.content: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И КОМПЈУТЕРСКО ИНЖЕНЕРСТВО 11.Coloured Petri nets Traditionally a modeling technique in mathematics, petri-nets are also useful for modeling business processes. Petri- nets classify or color-code complex workflow steps, users, and routes in different colors When a system has numerous processes that interact and synchronise with each other, then coloured Petri nets are ideal. This modelling technique is used to design, specify, simulate and verify systems. Petri nets are unique in that they can represent both a state – such as passive, unsent, or waiting – and an action – such as send, receive, or transmit – in the same diagram. Coloured nets use colours to differentiate their symbols, and use a formal, mathematical representation with well-defined syntax and semantics.

You want to learn more about the system to make an informed decision but the complexity of the system prevents you from doing that directly. Therefore you proceed indirectly by creating and studying another entity (the simulation model), which is sufficiently similar to the real-world system. Simulation can have many forms (for example, discrete-event simulation, continuous simulation, system dynamics, Monte-Carlo simulation, qualitative simulation, etc.).

slides.title: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И
slides.content: ФАКУЛТЕТ ЗА ИНФОРМАТИЧКИ НАУКИ И КОМПЈУТЕРСКО ИНЖЕНЕРСТВО TCO = “Total Cost of Ownership" TCO a type of calculation or business concept designed to help  managers assess the economic value of an investment through its cost. In the IT world, your investment is usually a system  (hardware/software) or a service. TCO calculations consist of both direct and indirect costs  Direct Costs: Are directly accountable to the investment.  Eg. Hardware, Software, Operation, and Admin. Costs Indirect Costs: Are not directly accountable to the  investment. Eg. End user operations (support), Downtime, Loss of Productivity

This is known as a TCO analysis.

OSS delivers lower Direct costs over proprietary software (due to ◼ reduced licensing costs). Seems obvious enough!  Several TCO studies claim OSS has higher indirect costs when ◼ compared to market-leading proprietary software. How are they able to make this claim? 

Is it better? C)If the marketing department claims that by spending $5,000 ◼ next year on local advertising they can generate an additional $9000 in sales boost sales Which option has the best ROI? ◼

slides.title: Introduction to
slides.content: Introduction to Microservices Riste Stojanov, PhD Building Microservices: Designing Fine-Grained Systems Chapter 1 & 2

slides.title: Introduction to Microservices
slides.content: Introduction to Microservices • Microservices are independently releasable services modeled around a business domain. • Encapsulates functionality and makes it accessible via networks. • Technology agnostic and offer many options for solving problems. • Type of service-oriented architecture with independent deployability. • Internal implementation details are hidden from the outside world. • Information hiding is key, allowing for clear separation between what can change easily and what is more difficult to change. • Changes inside a microservice boundary shouldn't affect upstream consumers. • Microservices avoid shared databases and instead use their own databases. • Microservices enable independent releasability of functionality and looser coupling.

slides.title: Key concepts
slides.content: Key concepts • Independent Deployability • Allows for changes to be made to a microservice without affecting other services • Leads to loosely coupled services • It's a discipline that should be adopted as the default release approach • Ensure loose coupling between microservices with explicit, well-defined, and stable contracts • Microservices and Data Ownership • Microservices should avoid shared databases – it makes independent deployability difficult • Each microservice should own its data • Accessing data from another microservice requires requesting it • Encapsulation is key to information hiding • Separation of internal implementation and external contract is crucial • Hiding internal state reduces backward-incompatible changes • Don't share databases unless necessary • Independent deployability relies on limited backward-incompatible changes

slides.title: Key concepts
slides.content: Key concepts Model around business domain • DDD promotes service boundaries around business domains • Makes it easier to roll out new functionality • Cross-service changes should be made as infrequent as possible • Microservices prioritize high cohesion of business functionality over technical functionality • Layered architectures can lead to inefficient changes in functionality • Services should be end-to-end slices of business functionality

slides.title: Key concepts
slides.content: Key concepts • Size Considerations • Lines of code is not a good measure due to language differences • A microservice should be as big as it can be easily understood • The goal is to have as small an interface as possible • Size is highly contextual and depends on team experience • Focus on handling complexity and defining microservice boundaries • Incremental migration to microservices is recommended • Don't worry about size, focus on manageability and understanding • Flexibility • Microservices provide flexibility on multiple axes: organizational, technical, scale, robustness • The cost of microservices architecture must be weighed against the benefits of flexibility • Adopting microservices is a gradual process, like turning a dial, rather than flipping a switch • Incremental adoption allows for assessment and adjustment of the impact as you go • Finding a balance between keeping options open and bearing the cost of microservices is crucial

slides.title: Key concepts
slides.content: Key concepts Alignment of Teams and Services • Organizations which design systems...are constrained to produce designs which are copies of their communication structures. • —Melvin Conway, “How Do Committees Invent?” • Traditional team structures can lead to inefficient hand-offs and slow down development • Technical separation in layered architectures • Stream-aligned teams own an end-to-end slice of user-facing functionality, enabling faster and more independent work • Microservices can encapsulate a thin slice of each tier (UI, application logic, data storage), making it easier to make changes and align teams with business domains

slides.title: Monoliths
slides.content: Monoliths • Single-Process Monolith • Entire system deployed as one process • Can scale by running multiple instances • Simple and effective for small teams and systems • Modular Monolith • Single-process deployment with modular code structure • Modules developed independently, deployed together • Easier to evolve than a flat monolith • Database decomposition often a challenge • Successfully used by large systems (e.g., Shopify) • Distributed Monolith • Multiple services, but tightly coupled and deployed together • Combines downsides of both monoliths and distributed systems • Lacks proper service boundaries, causing cross-service ripple effects

slides.title: Monoliths
slides.content: Monoliths Pros and Cons • Cons • Multiple developers working on the same code can cause conflicts • Different teams may want to push functionality live at different times • Confusion around ownership and decision-making can occur • Having a monolith does not guarantee delivery contention, but it can make it more likely • Microservice architecture can help reduce delivery contention by providing concrete boundaries for ownership • Pros • Simpler deployment topology • Avoid pitfalls associated with distributed systems • Simpler developer workflows and monitoring • Easier end-to-end testing and troubleshooting • All code is in one place, making it easier to use • Monolithic architecture is a valid choice • Should be considered as the sensible default architectural style • Microservices should be used only when justified

slides.title: Advantages of Microservices
slides.content: Advantages of Microservices Microservices achieve distributed systems benefits to a greater degree due to well-defined service boundaries Combines information hiding and domain-driven design with distributed systems Delivers significant gains over other forms of distributed architectures

slides.title: Technology Heterogeneity in Microservices
slides.content: Technology Heterogeneity in Microservices • Use of different technologies in each microservice • Right tool for each job, rather than a standardized approach • Improved performance by using a different technology stack • Easy adoption of new technologies and advancements • Reduced risk when trying out new technologies • Ability to limit potential negative impact • Overhead of embracing multiple technologies • Internal technology implementation is hidden from consumers

slides.title: Robustness in Microservices
slides.content: Robustness in Microservices • Bulkhead: isolating problems to prevent cascade failures • Service boundaries as bulkheads in microservices • Microservices can handle total failure of constituent services and degrade functionality • Networks and machines can fail, requiring handling and mitigation strategies • Distributed systems introduce new sources of failure

slides.title: Scaling Microservices
slides.content: Scaling Microservices • Monolithic services require scaling everything together • Microservices allow scaling of individual services that need it • Smaller services can run on smaller, less powerful and chipper hardware • On-demand provisioning systems enable scaling on demand • Cost savings through effective scaling

slides.title: Ease of Deployment with Microservices
slides.content: Ease of Deployment with Microservices • One-line change to a monolithic application requires full deployment • Microservices allow for independent deployment of individual services • Faster deployment and rollback with microservices • Reduced risk with smaller changes between releases • Organizations like Amazon and Netflix use microservices for faster software release

slides.title: Organizational Alignment with Microservices
slides.content: Organizational Alignment with Microservices • Large teams and codebases can lead to productivity issues • Smaller teams working on smaller codebases tend to be more productive • Microservices help align architecture to organization • Minimizes the number of people working on a single codebase • Allows for changing ownership of services as the organization changes

slides.title: Composability in Distributed Systems
slides.content: Composability in Distributed Systems • Distributed systems enable reuse of functionality • Microservices allow for consumption of functionality in different ways • Need to think about multiple channels: web, native app, mobile web, tablet app, wearable device • Microservices provide addressable seams in the system for outside parties • Enables building applications in different ways as circumstances change • Monolithic applications have limited coarse-grained seams

slides.title: Microservice Pain Points
slides.content: Microservice Pain Points Microservice architectures bring complexity Microservice architecture inherits distributed systems issues

slides.title: Developer Experience in Microservices
slides.content: Developer Experience in Microservices • More services can lead to a poor developer experience • Resource-intensive runtimes like JVM limit the number of microservices on a single machine • Limit to the number of things that can be run locally • Conversations about what to do when the entire system cannot be run on one machine • Extreme solutions involve developing in the cloud • Limited scope of which parts of a system a developer needs to work on is a more straightforward approach • Collective ownership model can be problematic if developers need to work on any part of the system

slides.title: Technology Overload and Cost Implications
slides.content: Technology Overload and Cost Implications • Technology Overhead • New technology for microservice architectures can be overwhelming • Not all new technology is necessary, balance breadth and complexity with costs • Introduce new technology gradually as needed • Avoid technology fetishism and focus on shipping features to users • Microservices introduce fundamental challenges like data consistency and latency • Cost Implications • Increased costs due to more processes, computers, network, storage, and software • Short-term slowdown in delivery of new functionality or need for additional personnel • Microservices can help increase profits by reaching more customers or developing more functionality in parallel

slides.title: Reporting in Monolithic and Microservice
slides.content: Reporting in Monolithic and Microservice Architectures • Monolithic systems have a single database for reporting • Stakeholders can run reports directly against the monolithic database • Microservice architectures have scattered data across multiple schemas • Reporting across all data is more difficult in microservices • Modern approaches to reporting include using streaming for real-time reporting • Publishing data from microservices into central reporting databases is an alternative

slides.title: Monitoring and Troubleshooting in Microservice
slides.content: Monitoring and Troubleshooting in Microservice Architecture • Microservice architecture has a more complex approach to monitoring • Failure mode is not binary, individual service instances can go down • CPU usage is harder to monitor with many processes • Requires tools like Grafana

slides.title: Security in Microservices
slides.content: Security in Microservices • More information flows over networks between services • Data is more vulnerable to • being observed in transit • to man-in-the-middle attacks • Need to protect data in transit • Need to protect microservice endpoints from unauthorized access

slides.title: Challenges of End-to-End Testing in Microservice
slides.content: Challenges of End-to-End Testing in Microservice Architecture • End-to-end tests cover a broad scope of functionality • Harder to set up and maintain • Increased complexity of end-to-end tests • Diminishing return on investment as microservice architecture grows • New forms of testing are needed, such as contract-driven testing or testing in production

slides.title: Latency in Microservice Architecture
slides.content: Latency in Microservice Architecture • Microservice architecture can increase latency due to distributed processing • Serialization, transmission, and deserialization over networks contribute to latency • Measuring exact impact on latency is difficult at design or coding phase • Distributed tracing tools like Jaeger can help measure end-to-end latency • Understanding acceptable latency for operations is necessary

slides.title: Data Consistency in Distributed Systems
slides.content: Data Consistency in Distributed Systems • Shifting from monolithic to distributed systems poses data consistency challenges • Database transactions are not easily applicable in distributed systems • Distributed transactions are highly problematic for coordinating state changes • Alternative concepts: sagas and eventual consistency • These concepts require fundamental changes in thinking about data • Assessing impact of changes in production is crucial

slides.title: Enabling technologies for microservices
slides.content: Enabling technologies for microservices Log Aggregation and Distributed Tracing • Implement log aggregation system as a prerequisite for microservice architecture • Collect and aggregate logs from all services for analysis and alerting • Use correlation IDs to isolate logs associated with a given flow of calls • Distributed tracing tools help analyze traces across multiple services and detect bottlenecks • Open source tools like Jaeger provide distributed tracing features • Commercial products like Lightstep and Honeycomb offer advanced monitoring capabilities

slides.title: Enabling technologies for microservices
slides.content: Enabling technologies for microservices Containers and Kubernetes • Run each microservice instance in isolation • Containers provide a lightweight way to provision isolated execution for service instances • Faster spin-up times for new container instances • More cost-effective for many architectures • Container orchestration platforms like Kubernetes manage containers across machines • Kubernetes provides robustness and throughput while making efficient use of underlying machines • Consider adopting containers and Kubernetes when managing deployment becomes a significant headache • Running your own Kubernetes cluster can be a significant amount of work

slides.title: Enabling technologies for microservices
slides.content: Enabling technologies for microservices • Streaming in Microservices • Need to share data between microservices • Move away from batch reporting operations • Apache Kafka: popular choice for streaming data • Kafka capabilities: message permanence, compaction, scalability • KSQLDB and Apache Flink for stream-processing • Debezium: open source tool for streaming data from existing datasources over Kafka • Public Cloud and Serverless • Public cloud providers offer managed services for application management • database instances, Kubernetes clusters, message brokers, and distributed file systems • Serverless products hide underlying machines, allowing higher-level abstraction • Message brokers, storage solutions, databases, Function as a Service (FaaS) platforms • FaaS platforms provide abstraction around code deployment, handling instance spinning up on demand

slides.title: Should I Use Microservices?
slides.content: Should I Use Microservices? Assess your problem space, skills, and technology landscape before deciding on microservices Understand what you are trying to achieve before adopting microservices Microservices are an architectural approach, not the only approach Context plays a huge part in deciding whether to use microservices Careful thought is required when considering microservices due to numerous challenges

slides.title: Whom Microservices Might Not Work For
slides.content: Whom Microservices Might Not Work For • Microservice architectures may not be suitable for brand-new products or startups due to changing domain models • Defining service boundaries can be expensive and may require significant changes • Startups typically have fewer people available to build the system, making microservices more challenging • Microservices bring new work and complexity, which can tie up valuable bandwidth • The 'microservice tax' can be difficult to justify for small teams • Organizations creating software for customer deployment may struggle with microservices due to added complexity • Customers may not have the necessary skills or technology to handle microservice deployments

slides.title: Where Microservices Work Well
slides.content: Where Microservices Work Well • Allow multiple developers to work independently on the same system • Suitable for Software as a Service (SaaS) applications with 24-7 operation • Enable independent releasability and scaling • Technology-agnostic, allowing for easy deployment on cloud platforms • Provide flexibility for evolving systems • Beneficial for organizations with growing development teams • Enable easy adoption of new technologies, such as FaaS platforms

slides.title: Data Strategy
slides.content: Data Strategy • “Data Leadership is about understanding the organization’s relationship with data and seeking ways to help the organization meet its goals using whatever tools are available,” – Anthony Algmin • To truly be an effective part of the business, the data architect should understand the answers to these questions: • What is our business operation’s goal? • What are we trying to accomplish as an entity? • What is the thing we should be doing as a business fundamentally? https://www.dataversity.net/

slides.title: Data Strategy
slides.content: Data Strategy • Answers to these questions lead to more detail about how to accomplish those goals: • How do we source our product? • How do we take those products to market? • How do we connect to customers? • How do we deliver products? • Next, an understanding of how data can support both the overarching goals and the processes used to reach them: • How do we leverage the data that we have today? • How do we create more data? • How do we use data to support all of these processes, measure them, and then improve them from a business perspective?

slides.title: Data Architecture
slides.content: Data Architecture • Start with the most valuable data! • How does this information contribute to the primary objectives of the organization? • Does the data pertain to specific teams or individuals and their goals? How? • How does this information bring the technological and “business” sides of the organization? • Can you use the data to draw specific, tangible, and usable insights to benefit the organization? • Data governance: How will you manage and control information in your architecture https://www.idashboards.com/blog/2018/12/12/data-architecture-building-and-managing-a-data- framework/

slides.title: Data Architecture
slides.content: Data Architecture • Instead of focusing on a framework that will last forever, focus on creating a data architecture that has the flexibility to grow with your organization. • Data exists within your organization to help key decision makers make informed choices. This means your data architecture should facilitate real- time information so stakeholders can access the data they want when they need it. • Data is service to users. Treat your users like customers who need service! • Bring your data to life. Account for representation and visualization!

slides.title: Stakeholders in Data Architecture
slides.content: Stakeholders in Data Architecture • Data architect (sometimes called big data architects)—defines the data vision based on business requirements, translates it to technology requirements, and defines data standards and principles. • Project manager—oversees projects that modify data flows or create new data flows. • Solution architect—designs data systems to meet business requirements. • Cloud architect or data centerengineer—prepares the infrastructure on which data systems will run, including storage solutions. • DBA or data engineer—builds data systems, populates them with data and takes care of data quality. • Data analyst—an end-user of the data architecture, uses it to create reports and manage an ongoing data feed for the business. • Data scientists—also a user of the data architecture, leveraging it to mine organizational data for fresh insights. https://blog.panoply.io/data-architecture-people-process-and-technology

slides.title: Data architecture frameworks
slides.content: Data architecture frameworks • There are several enterprise architecture frameworks that commonly serve as the foundation for building an organization's data architecture framework. • DAMA-DMBOK 2. DAMA International's Data Management Body of Knowledge is a framework specifically for data management. It provides standard definitions for data management functions, deliverables, roles, and other terminology, and presents guiding principles for data management. • Zachman Framework for Enterprise Architecture. The Zachman Framework is an enterprise ontology created by John Zachman at IBM in the 1980s. The "data" column of the Zachman Framework comprises multiple layers, including architectural standards important to the business, a semantic model or conceptual/enterprise data model, an enterprise/logical data model, a physical data model, and actual databases. • The Open Group Architecture Framework (TOGAF). TOGAF is an enterprise architecture methodology that offers a high-level framework for enterprise software development. Phase C of TOGAF covers developing a data architecture and building a data architecture roadmap.

slides.title: TOGAF Phase C1: Information Systems Architectures - Data Architecture -
slides.content: TOGAF Phase C1: Information Systems Architectures - Data Architecture - Approach - Key Considerations for Data Architecture • Data Governance • Ensures that the organisation has the necessary dimensions in place to enable the data transformation • Structure – ensures the organisation has the necessary structure and the standards bodies to manage data entity aspects of the transformation • Management System - ensures the organisation has the necessary management system and data-related programs to manage the governance aspects of data entities throughout its lifecycle • People - addresses what data-related skills and roles the organisation requires for the transformation

slides.title: Why the DMBOK2?
slides.content: Why the DMBOK2? • Data Management Body of Knowledge (DAMA-DMBOK Guide) is a collection of processes and best practices. • Contains generally accepted as best practices and references for each Data Management discipline. • Data Management (DM) is an overarching term that describes the processes used to plan, specify, enable, create, acquire, maintain, use, archive, retrieve, control, and purge data. • These processes overlap and interact within each data management knowledge area.

slides.title: What is the purpose of the DMBoK
slides.content: What is the purpose of the DMBoK • The current DM environment can be a confusing combination of terms, methods, tools, opinion, and hype. • To mature this discipline, DAMA International’s Guide to the Data Management Body of Knowledge (DAMA-DMBOK) provides concepts and capability maturity models for the standardization of: • Activities, processes, and best practices • Roles and responsibilities • Deliverables and metrics • A maturity model • Standardization of data management disciplines will help data management professionals perform more effectively and consistently.

slides.title: The 11 Data Management Knowledge Areas
slides.content: The 11 Data Management Knowledge Areas (According to DAMA DMBOK -2) • Data Governance – planning, oversight, and control over management of data and the use of data and data-related resources. While we understand that governance covers ‘processes’, not ‘things’, the common term is Data Governance, and so we will use this term. • Data Architecture – the overall structure of data and data-related resources as an integral part of the enterprise architecture • Data Modeling & Design (Data Implementation) – analysis, design, building, testing, and maintenance • Data Storage & Operations – structured physical data assets storage deployment and management • Data Security – ensuring privacy, confidentiality and appropriate access to PII, PHI and an individuals private data. Ensuring network security as well

slides.title: The 11 Data Management Knowledge
slides.content: The 11 Data Management Knowledge Areas(2) • Data Integration & Interoperability –acquisition, extraction, transformation, movement, delivery, replication, federation, virtualization and operational support • Documents & Content –storing, protecting, indexing, and enabling access to data found in unstructured sources (electronic files and physical records), and making this data available for integration and interoperability with structured (database) data. • Reference & Master Data –Managing shared data to reduce redundancy and ensure better data quality through standardized definition and use of data values. • Data Warehousing & Business Intelligence –managing analytical data processing and enabling access to decision support data for reporting and analysis. • Metadata –collecting, categorizing, maintaining, integrating, controlling, managing, and delivering metadata. • Data Quality –defining, monitoring, maintaining data integrity, and improving data quality.

slides.title: DMBOK Data Management Environmental
slides.content: DMBOK Data Management Environmental Elements • Goals and Principles -directional business goals of each function and the fundamental principles that guide performance of each function • Activities -each function is composed of lower level activities, sub-activities, tasks and steps • Primary Deliverables -information and physical databases and documents created as interim and final outputs of each function. Some deliverables are essential, some are generally recommended, and others are optional depending on circumstances • Roles and Responsibilities -business and IT roles involved in performing and supervising the function, and the specific responsibilities of each role in that function. Many roles will participate in multiple functions • Practices and Techniques -common and popular methods and procedures used to perform the processes and produce the deliverables and may also include common conventions, best practice recommendations, and alternative approaches without elaboration • Technology -categories of supporting technology such as software tools, standards and protocols, product selection criteria and learning curves • Organisation and Culture –this can include issues such as management metrics, critical success factors, reporting structures, budgeting, resource allocation issues, expectations and attitudes, style, cultural, approach to change management

slides.title: Modern Data Architectures
slides.content: Modern Data Architectures • Cloud-native: Modern data architectures are designed to support elastic scaling, high availability, end-to-end security for data in motion and data at rest, and cost and performance scalability • Scalable data pipelines: To take advantage of emerging technologies, data architectures support real- time data streaming and micro-batch data bursts • Seamless data integration: Data architectures integrate with legacy applications using standard API interfaces. They are optimised for sharing data across systems, geographies, and organisations • Real-time data enablement: Modern data architectures support the ability to deploy automated and active data validation, classification, management, and governance • Decoupled and extensible: Modern data architectures are designed to be loosely coupled, enabling services to perform minimal tasks independent of other services

slides.title: Data Integration Methodologies
slides.content: Data Integration Methodologies Manual data integration: Data managers must manually conduct all phases of the integration, from retrieval to presentation. Middleware data integration: Middleware, a type of software, facilitates communication between legacy systems and updated ones to expedite integration. Application-based integration: Software applications locate, retrieve, and integrate data by making data from different sources and systems compatible with one another. Uniform access integration: A technique that retrieves and uniformly displays data, but leaves it in its original source. Common storage integration: An approach that retrieves and uniformly displays the data, but also makes a copy of the data and stores it. https://www.talend.com/resources/data-integration-methods/

slides.title: Manual Data Integration
slides.content: Manual Data Integration • Pros: • Reduced cost: This technique requires little maintenance and typically only integrates a small number of data sources. • Greater freedom: The user has total control over the integration. • Cons: • Less access: A developer or manager must manually orchestrate each integration. • Difficulty scaling: Scaling for larger projects requires manually changing the code for each integration, and that takes time. • Greater room for error: A manager and/or analyst must handle the data at each stage. • This strategy is best for one-time instances, but it quickly becomes untenable for complex or recurring integrations because it is a very tedious, manual process. Everything from data collection, to cleaning, to presentation is done by hand, and those processes take time and resources.

slides.title: Middleware data integration
slides.content: Middleware data integration • Pros: • Better data streaming: The software conducts the integration automatically and in the same way each time. • Easier access between systems: The software is coded to facilitate communication between the systems in a network. • Cons: • Less access: The middleware needs to be deployed and maintained by a developer with technical knowledge. • Limited functionality: Middleware can only work with certain systems. • For businesses integrating legacy systems with more modern systems, middleware is ideal, but it’s mostly a communications tool and has limited capabilities for data analytics.

slides.title: Application-based integration
slides.content: Application-based integration • Pros: • Simplified processes: One application does all the work automatically. • Easier information exchange: The application allows systems and departments to transfer information seamlessly. • Fewer resources are used: Because much of the process is automated, managers and/or analysts can pursue other projects. • Cons: • Limited access: This technique requires special, technical knowledge and a data manager and/or analyst to oversee application deployment and maintenance. • Inconsistent results: The approach is unstandardized and varies from businesses offering this as a service. • Complicated setup: Designing the application(s) to work seamlessly across departments requires developers, managers, and/or analysts with technical knowledge. • Difficult data management: Accessing different systems can lead to compromised data integrity. • Sometimes this approach is called enterprise application integration, because it’s common in enterprises working in hybrid cloud environments. These businesses need to work with multiple data sources —on-premises and in the cloud. This approach optimizes data and workflows between these environments.

slides.title: Uniform access integration
slides.content: Uniform access integration • Pros: • Lower storage requirements: There is no need to create a separate place to store data. • Easier data access: This approach works well with multiple systems and data sources. • Simplified view of data: This technique creates a uniform appearance of data for the end user. • Cons: • Data integrity challenges: Accessing so many sources can lead to compromising data integrity. • Strained systems: Data host systems are not usually designed to handle the amount and frequency of data requests in this process. • For businesses needing to access multiple, disparate systems, this is an optimal approach. If the data request isn’t too burdensome for the host system, this approach can yield insights without the cost of creating a backup or copy of the data.

slides.title: Common storage integration
slides.content: Common storage integration • Pros: • Reduced burden: The host system isn’t constantly handling data queries. • Increased data version management control: Accessing data from one source, versus multiple disparate sources, leads to better data integrity. • Cleaner data appearance: The stored copy of data allows managers and/or analysts to run numerous queries while maintaining uniformity in the data’s appearance. • Enhanced data analytics: Maintaining a stored copy allows manager and/or analysts to run more sophisticated queries without worrying about compromised data integrity. • Cons: • Increased storage costs: Creating a copy of the data means finding and paying for a place to store it. • Higher maintenance costs: Orchestrating this approach requires technical experts to set up the integration, oversee, and maintain it. • Common storage is the most sophisticated integration approach. If businesses have the resources, this is almost certainly thebest approach, because it allows for the most sophisticated queries. That sophistication can lead to deeper insights.

slides.content: When to use which approach? Data integration approach When to use it Manual data integration Merge data for basic analysis between a small amount of data sources Automate and translate communication between legacy and modernized Middleware data integration systems Automate and translate communication between systems and allow for more Application-based integration complicated data analysis Automate and translate communication between systems and present the data Uniform access integration uniformly to allow for complicated data analysis Present the data uniformly, create and store a copy, and perform the most Common storage integration sophisticated data analysis tasks

slides.title: Modeling Microservices
slides.content: Modeling Microservices Riste Stojanov, PhD

slides.title: Modeling Microservices
slides.content: Modeling Microservices • Foundational concepts: • information hiding • coupling • cohesion • Domain-driven design • Drawing boundaries around microservices • Maximizing benefits and avoiding downsides

slides.title: What Makes a Good Microservice Boundary?
slides.content: What Makes a Good Microservice Boundary? • Microservices should be changed and deployed independently • Ability to change one microservice in isolation from another is vital • Three key concepts for good microservice boundary: information hiding, cohesion, and coupling • Microservices are a form of modular decomposition with network-based interaction

slides.title: Information Hiding and Microservice Boundaries
slides.content: Information Hiding and Microservice Boundaries • Information hiding: hide as many details as possible behind a module boundary • Benefits of modular architecture: • improved development time, • comprehensibility, • flexibility • Modules can be developed independently and changed without affecting other modules • Reducing assumptions between modules improves connections and allows for safer changes • Information hiding applies to microservices, with the added benefit of independent deployment

slides.title: Cohesion in Microservice Architecture
slides.content: Cohesion in Microservice Architecture • Code that changes together, stays together • Group related functionality to minimize changes in multiple places • Unrelated behavior should be separated • Aim for strong cohesion in microservice architectures • Find boundaries in the problem domain to ensure related behavior is in one place • Loose communication between boundaries is desirable

slides.title: Loose Coupling in Microservices
slides.content: Loose Coupling in Microservices • Loosely coupled services allow for independent changes and deployment • Tight coupling occurs when a change to one service requires a change to another • Integration styles can cause tight coupling between services • A loosely coupled service has limited knowledge of other services • Chatty communication can lead to tight coupling

slides.title: The Interplay of Coupling and Cohesion
slides.content: The Interplay of Coupling and Cohesion • Coupling and cohesion are related concepts in system design • Constantine's law states that a structure is stable if cohesion is strong and coupling is low • Stability in microservice boundaries is crucial for independent deployability • Coupling describes the relationship between things across a boundary • Cohesion applies to the relationship between things inside a boundary • There is no absolute best way to organize code, only trade-offs between coupling and cohesion • The right balance between coupling and cohesion depends on context and system requirements • System requirements can change, requiring revisiting of design decisions

slides.title: Types of Coupling
slides.content: Types of Coupling • Different forms of coupling have been studied in structured programming • These concepts can be applied to microservice-based systemsTypes of coupling can be organized from low (desirable) to high (undesirable)

slides.title: Domain Coupling
slides.content: Domain Coupling • Domain coupling: one microservice depends on another for functionality • Types of coupling are unavoidable in microservice architecture • Minimize domain coupling to avoid single microservice depending on multiple downstream services • Domain coupling introduces Temporal coupling • concepts bundled together due to simultaneous occurrence • Temporal coupling can cause issues with resource contention and scalability • Asynchronous communication can help avoid temporal coupling

slides.title: Pass-through Coupling
slides.content: Pass-through Coupling • Pass-through coupling: one microservice passes data to another purely because it's needed by a downstream service • Example: Order Processor sends Shipping Manifest to Warehouse, which passes it to Shipping microservice • Problem: change to required data downstream can cause significant upstream changes • Solution 1: bypass intermediary (e.g., Order Processor speaks directly to Shipping) • Solution 2: hide requirement for Shipping Manifest from Order Processor (e.g., Warehouse constructs manifest locally) • Solution 3: treat Shipping Manifest as a blob of data, without processing it in Warehouse

slides.title: Common Coupling
slides.content: Common Coupling • Occurs when two or more microservices use a common set of data • Examples: shared database, shared memory, shared filesystem • Changes to the structure of the data can impact multiple microservices at once • Can lead to resource contention and operational problems • Types of common coupling: static reference data, dynamic data • Static reference data is relatively benign, but dynamic data can be problematic • Use of finite state machines can help manage state transitions • Single microservice should manage the order state to avoid conflicts • Requests to a microservice should be seen as requests that can be rejected if invalid

slides.title: Content Coupling
slides.content: Content Coupling • Content coupling occurs when an upstream service changes the internal state of a downstream service • This often happens when an external service accesses another microservice's database directly • It can lead to duplication of logic and inconsistent data • The lines of ownership become less clear • Exposing internal data structures to outside parties can make changes more difficult • Avoid content coupling by having services communicate through requests rather than direct database access

slides.title: Alternatives to Business Domain Boundaries
slides.content: Alternatives to Business Domain Boundaries • DDD is useful for building microservice architectures • Multiple methods can be used in conjunction with DDD to identify boundaries • Other factors should be considered when finding microservice boundaries

slides.title: Volatility-Based Decomposition
slides.content: Volatility-Based Decomposition • Volatility-based decomposition identifies parts of the system undergoing frequent change • Extracts changing functionality into separate services for more effective work • Not a one-size-fits-all approach, especially when considering different drivers like scalability • Bimodal IT categorizes systems into Mode 1 (Systems of Record) and Mode 2 (Systems of Innovation) • Mode 1 systems are slow-changing, while Mode 2 systems require fast changes and business involvement • Bimodal IT can oversimplify and lead to avoiding necessary changes • Changes in functionality often require updates to both Systems of Record and Systems of Innovation • Volatility-based decomposition can be useful for determining boundaries when time-to- market is key • Goal determines the most appropriate mechanism for decomposition

slides.title: Data-Driven Decomposition
slides.content: Data-Driven Decomposition • The nature of data drives decomposition • Personally identifiable information (PII) affects system design • Payment Card Industry (PCI) standards require specific data management • Splitting systems to limit oversight and compliance • Segregating data for privacy and security concerns

slides.title: Technology Boundaries
slides.content: Technology Boundaries • Using different technologies can be a factor in finding boundaries • Mixing runtime models can be challenging • Different databases can be accommodated in a single microservice • Classic three-tiered architecture is often driven by technological boundaries

slides.title: Organizational Structure and Service Boundaries
slides.content: Organizational Structure and Service Boundaries • Organizational structure affects system architecture • Service boundaries should align with team ownership • Shared ownership of microservices can be problematic • Changes in organizational structure may require rearchitecting software • Layering within a microservice boundary can be sensible, but not across boundaries

slides.title: Summary
slides.content: Summary • Microservices are not the goal, but a means to achieve the goal • Adopting microservices should be a conscious decision based on rational thinking • There are alternative solutions to scaling, such as load balancing

slides.title: Microservice Communication
slides.content: Microservice Communication Styles Riste Stojanov, PhD

slides.title: From In-Process to Inter-Process
slides.content: From In-Process to Inter-Process • Calls between different processes across a network (inter-process) are different from calls within a single process (in-process) • In-process calls occur within a single process • In-process calls have less overhead compared to inter-process calls • Changes to an interface within a process are straightforward • Inter-process calls involve communication via a network • APIs designed for in-process use may not be suitable for inter-process situations • Passing data between microservices requires serialization and deserialization • Data size and serialization mechanisms can impact performance • Developers should be aware of network calls to avoid performance bottlenecks • Backward-incompatible changes require lockstep deployment or phased rollout • Consumers must be updated to use the new interface

slides.title: Technology for Inter-Process Communication
slides.content: Technology for Inter-Process Communication • Range of technology for inter-process communication is vast • Too many choices can be overburdening • People often choose familiar or latest technology without considering the problem • Specific technology choice comes with a set of ideas and constraints that may not be suitable for the problem being solved • Examples of misused technologies: Angular/React for websites, Kafka for request- response • Importance of considering communication style before choosing technology

slides.title: Microservice Communication Styles
slides.content: Microservice Communication Styles • Synchronous blocking: microservice • Microservice architecture makes a call and blocks operation • may have a mix of collaboration styles • Request-response and event-driven are waiting for the response common collaboration styles • Asynchronous nonblocking: microservice emits a call and carries on processing • Request-response: microservice sends a request and expects a response • Event-driven: microservices emit events, which other microservices consume and react to • Common data: microservices collaborate via shared data source

slides.title: Synchronous Blocking Pattern
slides.content: Synchronous Blocking Pattern • A microservice sends a call to a downstream process and blocks until the call is completed • The result of the call may be needed for further operations or to verify the call was successful • Synchronous blocking calls are often request-response calls • Advantages • Familiar programming style • Synchronous calls are simple and easy to understand. Similar to inter-process calls in less distributed architectures • Disadvantages • Temporal coupling between microservices • Downstream microservice needs to be reachable for the call to work. • Upstream microservice needs to handle compensating actions • Response sent over the same inbound network connection • System vulnerable to cascading issues caused by downstream outages

slides.title: Synchronous Blocking Calls in Microservice
slides.content: Synchronous Blocking Calls in Microservice Architectures • Synchronous blocking calls can be suitable for simple microservice architectures • They become problematic with longer chains of calls, increasing the risk of failure and resource contention • Issues in any involved microservice or network call can cause the whole operation to fail • Long chains of synchronous calls can lead to significant resource contention and increased latency • Reexamining interactions between microservices can help improve the situation • Moving certain tasks, like Fraud Detection, to background processes can reduce concerns around call chain length • Replacing blocking calls with non-blocking interactions is an alternative approach • Reducing call chain length improves overall latency and reduces dependencies

slides.title: Asynchronous Nonblocking Pattern
slides.content: Asynchronous Nonblocking Pattern • Asynchronous communication doesn't block the microservice issuing the call • Three common styles: • Communication through common data: upstream microservice changes common data for other microservices to use • Request-response: microservice sends a request and receives a response when the operation completes • Event-driven interaction: microservice broadcasts an event for other microservices to react to • When to use • Long-running processes are a good candidate for asynchronous communication • Situations with long call chains that can’t be easily restructured

slides.title: Asynchronous Communication
slides.content: Asynchronous Communication Advantages Disadvantages • Avoids temporal coupling concerns • Higher level of complexity • Range of choice can be overwhelming • Beneficial for long-running processes • Difficult to adopt if it doesn't map to • Enables nonblocking calls for time- your mental models of computing consuming tasks • Potential for trouble in implementation • Async/await can be used in a blocking, synchronous style • Promises can resolve to a state at some point in the future

slides.title: Communication Through Common Data
slides.content: Communication Through Common Data • A style of communication that spans a multitude of implementations • One microservice puts data into a defined location, and another microservice makes use of the data • Fundamentally asynchronous in nature • Example: New Product Importer creates a file for downstream Inventory and Catalog microservices • When to use it • Enabling interoperability between processes with technology restrictions • Sharing large volumes of data, such as multigigabyte files or millions of database rows • Suitable for older systems with limitations on supported technologies • Can be used with widely supported data store technologies, like file systems

slides.title: Implementation of Communication Through
slides.content: Implementation of Communication Through Common Data • Persistent store for data is required • File-system can be used as a simple solution • Distributed memory store can also be used • Downstream microservices need mechanism to identify new data • Polling is a common solution to this problem • Data lake and data warehouse are two common examples of this pattern • Data lake: sources upload raw data, consumers process it • Data warehouse: structured data store, microservices push data in known format • Unidirectional flow of information makes it easier to reason about the system

slides.title: Communication Through Common Data
slides.content: Communication Through Common Data Advantages Disadvantages • Polling mechanism may not be • Simple to implement suitable for low-latency situations • Uses commonly understood • Combining with other call-informing mechanisms can reduce latency technology • Streaming technology like Kafka is a • Enables interoperability between better fit for real-time processing different systems • Common data store can become a source of coupling between • Handles large data volumes microservices effectively • Changes to the data store structure can break communication between microservices

slides.title: Request-Response Communication Pattern
slides.content: Request-Response Communication Pattern • Interaction can be undertaken via synchronous blocking call or asynchronous non-blocking fashion • Queues help buffer requests when they can’t be handled quickly enough • Need to relate responses to original requests • State associated with original request can be stored in a database • Time-out handling is necessary to avoid blocking issues • When to use it • Used when calls need to be completed in a certain order • If a call didn't work to carry out compensating actions

slides.title: Event-Driven Communication Pattern
slides.content: Event-Driven Communication Pattern • A microservice emits events that may or may not be received by other microservices • The event emitter has no knowledge of the intent of other microservices to use the event • Events are statements about something that has occurred within the emitting microservice • Event-driven interactions are more loosely coupled compared to request-response calls • This pattern reduces domain coupling and allows for more autonomous teams • Events and messages are related but distinct concepts: an event is a fact, while a message is a medium for transmitting events or requests

slides.title: Implementing Event-Driven Microservices
slides.content: Implementing Event-Driven Microservices • Two main aspects to consider: • event emission and consumer notification • Message brokers like RabbitMQ handle both problems • Producers publish events to the broker, which handles subscriptions • Brokers can handle consumer state, ensuring messages are not duplicated • Using HTTP (e.g., Atom) as an alternative for propagating events • Atom allows reusing existing specifications and libraries • HTTP handles scale well, but may not be suitable for low-latency use cases • Consider using a message broker if available, otherwise consider Atom • Be aware of the sunk cost fallacy when implementing custom solutions

slides.title: What's in an Event?
slides.content: What's in an Event? • An event informs interested parties about a specific occurrence • Two types of events: Just an ID or Fully detailed events • Just an ID: contains only an identifier for the newly registered customer • Fully detailed events: contain all necessary information, allowing for looser coupling • Events with more information can double as historical records and aid in auditing or event sourcing • Concerns about event size and data sensitivity should be considered when designing events

slides.title: Event-Driven Collaboration
slides.content: Event-Driven Collaboration • Thrives in situations where information needs to be broadcast • Useful when inverting intent and letting downstream microservices work out the details • Suitable for loose coupling • Introduces new sources of complexity • Can be used in combination with other interaction styles • More teams are replacing request-response interactions with event-driven interactions

slides.title: Proceed with Caution: Asynchronous
slides.content: Proceed with Caution: Asynchronous Programming and Event-Driven Architectures • Asynchronous programming can lead to more decoupled, scalable systems • However, it also increases complexity in managing publishing and subscribing to messages • Long-running async request-response requires considering what to do when the response comes back • Short-lived async can be easier to manage with the right APIs, but is a different way of thinking for programmers • Specifying a maximum retry limit for jobs on queues is crucial • Implementing a message hospital (or dead letter queue) to view and replay bad messages is necessary • Correlation IDs can help trace requests across process boundaries • Monitoring and logging are essential in event-driven architectures

slides.title: Summary
slides.content: Summary • Choose technology based on communication style • Ensure backward compatibility • Validate changes before deployment

slides.title: What is a Data Warehouse?
slides.content: What is a Data Warehouse? A Practitioners Viewpoint “A data warehouse is simply a single, complete, and consistent store of data obtained from a variety of sources and made available to end users in a way they can understand and use it in a business context.” -- Barry Devlin, IBM Consultant

slides.title: Data Warehouse
slides.content: Data Warehouse • Supports information processing by providing a solid platform of consolidated, historical data for analysis. • Designed to get data out and analyze quickly • A data warehouse is: – Subject-oriented : Contains information regarding objects of interest for decision support: Sales by region, by product, etc. – Integrated: Data are typically extracted from multiple, heterogeneous data sources (e.g., from sales, inventory, billing DBs etc.) - ETL (see later). – Time-variant: Contain historical data, longer horizon than operational system. – Nonvolatile : Physically separate store, data is not (or rarely) directly updated. -- W.H. Inmon, Building the Data Warehouse, 1992

slides.title: A Data Warehouse is...
slides.content: A Data Warehouse is... • Stored collection of diverse data • A solution to data integration problem • Single repository of information • Subject-oriented • Organized by subject, not by application • Used for analysis, data mining, etc. • Optimized differently from transaction-oriented db • User interface aimed at executive

slides.title: A Data Warehouse is…
slides.content: A Data Warehouse is… • Large volume of data (Gb, Tb) • Non-volatile • Historical • Time attributes are important • Updates infrequent • May be append-only • Examples • All transactions ever at Sainsbury’s • Complete client histories at insurance firm • LSE financial information and portfolios

slides.title: Dimension Tables
slides.content: Dimension Tables • Dimension tables have the following characteristics: • Hold descriptive information about a particular business perspective • Contain relatively static data • Are joined to a fact table through a foreign key reference

slides.title: Fact Tables
slides.content: Fact Tables • Fact tables have the following characteristics: • Contain numeric metrics of the business • Can contain one or more calculated measures • Records are updated not deleted. • May contain summarized (aggregated) data • Often contain date-stamped data • Key value is a composite key made up of the primary keys of the dimensions • Joined to dimension tables through foreign keys that reference primary keys in the dimension tables

slides.title: Typical OLAP Operations
slides.content: Typical OLAP Operations • Roll up (drill-up): summarize data • by climbing up hierarchy or by dimension reduction • Drill down (roll down): reverse of roll-up • from higher level summary to lower level summary or detailed data, or introducing new dimensions • Slice and dice: project and select • Pivot (rotate): • reorient the cube, visualization, 3D to series of 2D planes • Other operations • drill across: involving (across) more than one fact table • drill through: through the bottom level of the cube to its back-end relational tables (using SQL)

slides.title: OLAP: Data Cube Operations
slides.content: OLAP: Data Cube Operations • Slicing: Selecting the dimensions of the cube to be viewed. – Example: View “Sales volume” as a function of “Product ” by “Country “by “Quarter” • Dicing: Specifying the values along one or more dimensions. – Example: View “Sales volume” for “Product=PC” by “Country “by “Quarter”

slides.title: OLAP: Data Cube Operations
slides.content: OLAP: Data Cube Operations • Drilling down: from higher level aggregation to lower level aggregation or detailed data (Viewing by “state” after viewing by “region” ) • Rolling-up: Summarize data by climbing up hierarchy or by dimension reduction (E.g., viewing by “region” instead of by “state”)

slides.title: Implementing Microservice
slides.content: Implementing Microservice Communication Riste Stojanov, PhD

slides.title: Choosing the Ideal Technology
slides.content: Choosing the Ideal Technology • Backward Compatibility in Microservices • Making Services Simple for Consumers • Ensure technology allows for backward- • Allow clients full freedom in their compatible changes technology choice • Adding new fields shouldn't break clients • Providing a client library can ease adoption • Ability to validate changes for backward • Client libraries can increase coupling compatibility • Balance between ease of use and coupling • Get feedback before deploying to • Hide Internal Implementation Detail production • Increased coupling leads to higher cost of • Explicit Microservice Interface change • Interface should be explicit to consumers • Avoid technologies that push exposure of and developers internal representation detail • Use of explicit schema is strongly • Less technical debt within the service encouraged • Supporting documentation should be provided for clarity • Keep APIs Technology Agnostic • Avoid integration technology that dictates technology stacks

slides.title: Technology Choices
slides.content: Technology Choices • Remote procedure calls (e.g. SOAP, gRPC) • REST (architectural style with resources and verbs) • GraphQL (protocol for custom queries) • Message brokers (middleware for asynchronous communication)

slides.title: Challenges and Best Practices for RPC
slides.content: Challenges and Best Practices for RPC • RPC can be a good choice, but be aware of potential pitfalls • Don't abstract remote calls to the point that the network is completely hidden • Ensure server interface can evolve without requiring lockstep upgrades for clients • Finding the right balance for client code is important • gRPC is a recommended option due to its performance and ease of use

slides.title: REST over HTTP
slides.content: REST over HTTP • Widely used and understood interface style • Guarantees interoperability from a huge variety of technologies • Excels in situations where large-scale caching is desired • Suitable for exposing APIs to external parties or client interfaces • May suffer compared to more efficient communication protocols

slides.title: Introduction to GraphQL
slides.content: Introduction to GraphQL • Allows client-side devices to define queries and avoid multiple requests • Improves performance of constrained client-side devices • Reduces the need for server-side aggregation • GraphQL endpoint exposes a schema for client devices to use • Challenges include lack of language support, dynamic queries causing load on servers, and caching complexity • GraphQL is suited for use at the perimeter of the system, exposing functionality to external clients • Alternative patterns like backend for frontend (BFF) can be considered

slides.title: Message Brokers and Kafka
slides.content: Message Brokers and Kafka • Message brokers are used for decoupling microservices • Popular message brokers include RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, and Kafka • Kafka • Designed for large scale and has features like message permanence • Built-in support for stream processing using KSQL • At least once delivery • Message brokers provide a way to handle messages that are not processed immediately

slides.title: Serialization Formats
slides.content: Serialization Formats • Textual formats • Provide flexibility for clients with readability and interoperability • JSON has become the most popular text serialization format • Avro is a schema-based format that uses JSON as an underlying structure • XML is still a viable option with better tool support in some areas • Binary Formats • Used for efficient payload size and reading/writing • gRPC’s Protocol buffers are a popular binary serialization format for microservice-based communication • Other binary formats include Simple Binary Encoding, Cap’n Proto, and FlatBuffers • Benchmarks may not represent real-world usage, so comparison is recommended • Optimizations are rarely necessary, but important for ultra-low-latency distributed systems

slides.title: Schemas for Microservice Endpoints
slides.content: Schemas for Microservice Endpoints • Schemas define what endpoints expose • Contract breakages can be categorized and accept into two types: structural and semantic • Structural breakage: change in endpoint • Different types of schemas: XML Schema structure, e.g., fields/methods removal or Definition (XSD), JSON Schema addition of new required fields • Explicit schemas make life easier for • Example: changing method parameters (e.g., from two integers to one) developers and consumers • Semantic breakage: change in behavior • Schemas reduce the need for without changing the endpoint structure documentation • Example: changing calculation method from addition to multiplication • Schemas help catch accidental breakages • Testing is required to catch semantic of microservice endpoints breakages • Explicit schemas can aid communication between teams and serve as a safety net

slides.title: Handling Change Between Microservices
slides.content: Handling Change Between Microservices • Versioning is not just about numbering schemes, but also about handling contract changes • There are two topics in handling change: • Avoiding breaking changes • Managing breaking changes

slides.title: Avoiding Breaking Changes in Microservices
slides.content: Avoiding Breaking Changes in Microservices • Expansion changes: Add new things to a microservice interface, don’t remove old things • Tolerant reader: Be flexible in what you expect when consuming a microservice interface • Ignore changes that are not relevant • Postel’s law: Be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others • Right technology: Pick technology that makes it easier to make backward-compatible changes • Some technologies are more brittle when changing interfaces (e.g., Java RMI) • Other implementations make it easy to change without breaking clients • Protocol buffers (gRPC serialization format) use field numbers for flexibility • Avro sends schema with payload for dynamic interpretation • REST's HATEOAS enables clients to adapt to changing endpoints • Explicit interface: Be explicit about what a microservice exposes • Makes boundariesof information hiding more explicit • RESTtypically views schema as optional • OpenAPIand JSON Schema are gaining traction • Asynchronous messaging protocols struggle with explicit interfaces, but AsyncAPI and CloudEventsare emerging • Semantic versioning allows clients to know if they can integrate with a service based on version number

slides.title: Catch Accidental Breaking Changes Early
slides.content: Catch Accidental Breaking Changes Early • Pick up changes that will break consumers as soon as possible • Use schemas to pick up structural changes • Schema comparison tools help catch structural breakages • Tooling options: Protolock, json-schema-diff-validator, openapi-diff • Open source Confluent Schema Registry supports JSON Schema, Avro, and protocol buffers • Consumer-driven contract testing helps with semantic breakages • Testing is crucial if schemas are not used • Run tests using each supported client library against the latest service • Avoid or embrace breaks and have conversations with consuming services

slides.title: Managing Breaking Changes
slides.content: Managing Breaking Changes • Lockstep deployment: change microservice and consumers at the same time • Coexist incompatible microservice versions: run old and new versions side by side • Emulate the old interface: expose new interface and emulate old interface

slides.title: Approach Preferences for Microservices
slides.content: Approach Preferences for Microservices • Lockstep release can be justifiable in limited situations with a single team • Limitation of independent deployability • Need for consumers to upgrade to new interface • Lockstep deployments should be avoided to prevent a distributed monolith • Coexisting different versions of the same microservice can be problematic • Managing multiple versions • Directing consumers to the right microservice • Persistent state management • Coexistence may be acceptable for short periods, such as during blue-green deployment or canary release • Emulation of old endpoints is generally preferred over coexisting microservice versions

slides.title: The Social Contract in Microservices
slides.content: The Social Contract in Microservices • Balance between microservice maintainers' and consumers' needs • Discuss how backward-incompatible changes will be handled • Define how to raise issues, collaborate on changes, and update consumers • Agree on timeframe for consumers to shift to new interface • Consider consumer-first approach and potential financial implications • Tracking Usage and Managing Breaking Changes • Agree on a time for consumers to stop using the old interface • Implement logging for each endpoint to track usage • Use client identifiers to communicate with teams that need to migrate • Require clients to identify themselves through API gateways or user-agent headers

slides.title: Extreme Measures for Interface Deprecation
slides.content: Extreme Measures for Interface Deprecation • Talk to consumers using old interfaces and offer assistance to upgrade • Set a deadline (e.g., one year) for retiring old interfaces • Consider tracking usage of old interfaces before deprecation • Inserting delays or errors into old interfaces can encourage upgrades • Ensure all reasonable efforts have been made before taking extreme measures • Extreme measures may lead to inefficiency and should be used with caution • Communication and cooperation with consumers are key to successful deprecation

slides.title: DRY Principle in Microservices (Sharing Code via
slides.content: DRY Principle in Microservices (Sharing Code via Libraries) • DRY: Don't Repeat Yourself • Avoid duplicating system behavior and knowledge • Advantages • Reduces codebase size and improves maintainability • Helps prevent bugs due to forgotten changes • Use of shared code should not leak outside service boundary • Disadvantages • Shared code can create coupling if not used carefully • Updating library versions can lead to widespread deployment headaches • Multiple versions of the same library might be in use at the same time • Client libraries should be written by a separate team or community • Clients should be in charge of when to upgrade their client libraries

slides.title: Service Discovery
slides.content: Service Discovery • Knowing where microservices are located • Monitoring and finding available APIs • Service discovery handles instance registration and service lookup • Solutions should cope with constantly destroying and deploying new instances

slides.title: Domain Name System (DNS)
slides.content: Domain Name System (DNS) • DNS associates a name with the IP address of one or more machines • Entry point to the IP address of the host running a microservice or a load balancer • Handle updating DNS entries as part of deploying a service • Convention-based domain template: <servicename>- <environment>.musiccorp.net • Advantages: well-understood and well- used standard, widely supported • Disadvantages: updating DNS entries can be painful, DNS entries have a time to live (TTL) • Using a load balancer can help avoid stale DNS entries

slides.title: Dynamic Service Registries
slides.content: Dynamic Service Registries • Eureka: Netflix’s service registry (maintenance, no new features) • ZooKeeper: a centralized service registry • Consul: a modern service registry with health checking and load balancing • Kubernetes: an container orchestration platform with built-in service discovery • etcd: a distributed key-value store for service discovery • Rolling your own: using cloud provider APIs or custom solutions

slides.title: API Gateways
slides.content: API Gateways • Entry points for clients to access a system • They can handle tasks such as authentication, rate limiting, and routing • Should be kept simple and without complex business logic • Call aggregation and protocol rewriting should not be done in API gateways • API gateways can introduce additional latency and overhead if used for inter-microservice calls

slides.title: Service Meshes
slides.content: Service Meshes • Service meshes provide a configurable infrastructure layer for microservices • They offer features mutual TLS, correlation IDs, service discovery and load balancing • Popular service mesh options include Linkerd, Istio, and Envoy • Limitations • API gateways and service meshes primarily handle HTTP-related calls • REST, SOAP, gRPC can be managed via these products • Other protocols like message brokers (e.g., Kafka) may bypass the service mesh • Communication is done directly with the broker, not through the service mesh • Service mesh be assumed to work as an intermedicannotary for all calls

slides.title: Documenting Services
slides.content: Documenting Services • Documentation is necessary to understand API usage • Ideally, documentation should be up-to-date with the microservice API • Easy access to documentation when a service endpoint is known

slides.title: Explicit Schemas and Documentation
slides.content: Explicit Schemas and Documentation • Explicit schemas help understand endpoint structure but not behavior • Good documentation is still required to communicate endpoint usage • Without an explicit schema, documentation must explain structure and interface details • OpenAPI provides effective documentation and supports various tools • AsyncAPI and CloudEvents support documenting event-based interfaces • CloudEvents has gained popularity due to its association with CNCF and integration support
